listeningParts.title: Renting a flat
listeningParts.contextDescription: A student phones a letting agency about a flat advertised online.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Good morning, Riverside Lettings, Mia speaking.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Hi, I'm calling about one of the flats on your website. It's the two-bedroom one in Albert Street.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Ah yes, number twelve. It's a lovely flat, just been redecorated. Are you looking for yourself?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: For me and a friend. We're both starting a master's course in September, so we need somewhere for at least a year.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: That fits nicely. The landlord prefers a twelve-month tenancy anyway. Can I take your name first?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Sure. It's Tomás Ruiz. R-U-I-Z.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Thanks, Tomás. And a contact number?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: It's oh-seven-seven-one-four, three-six-two, nine-eight-five.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Lovely. So, let me tell you a bit about the flat. It's on the second floor of a converted Victorian house. There's no lift, I'm afraid, but there are only two flights of stairs.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: That's fine. Is it quiet? My friend is a light sleeper.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: It's a residential street, so there's not much traffic at night. The flat at the back looks over the gardens, and that's where both bedrooms are, so I'd say it's very quiet. The previous tenants were there for three years and never complained.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Good to hear. And is there a washing machine?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Yes, there's a washing machine in the kitchen, and a small drying rack, but no dryer.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: That's fine. The advert said the rent was eight hundred and fifty pounds a month. Is that right?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: It was, but the landlord has just put in a new kitchen, so it's now nine hundred and twenty a month. That's for the whole flat, not each.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Okay, so four hundred and sixty each. Does that include bills?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Water is included, but you'd pay for gas and electricity yourselves. Internet's included too; the landlord has a contract with a provider for the whole building.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Good. And is it furnished?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Partly furnished. Both bedrooms have a bed and a wardrobe, and there's a sofa and a dining table in the living room. But there are no desks, so if you're students, you'd probably want to buy those.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Right, desks. I'll note that. What about the area? I don't really know that part of town.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: It's very convenient. There's a supermarket on the corner, and the train station is about ten minutes' walk. If you're at the university, you can get the number fourteen bus, which goes right past the main library.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Perfect. Is there anywhere to keep a bike? I cycle most places.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: There's no garage, but there's a shed in the back garden that tenants share. Most people keep their bikes there.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Great. And what would we need to pay at the start?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: There's a deposit equal to five weeks' rent, which is protected in a government scheme and returned at the end of the tenancy, as long as there's no damage. You'd also pay the first month's rent in advance. We don't charge any agency fees; that's not allowed any more.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: That's good to know. Would we need a guarantor?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: For students, yes, usually. That's someone who agrees to pay the rent if you can't, normally a parent. If you don't have anyone in the UK, the landlord will accept six months' rent paid in advance instead.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: My parents are abroad, so we might have to do that. Can we see the flat?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Of course. I've got viewings on Wednesday afternoon. Could you do three o'clock?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Wednesday's difficult, I've got a class. Is Thursday possible?

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Thursday at eleven? I'm meeting another tenant nearby, so that works for me.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Eleven on Thursday is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Agent
dialogue.text: Great. Please bring some photo identification, a passport is best, and if you can, a letter from the university confirming your place. It speeds things up if you decide to take it.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Okay. Passport and university letter. Thanks so much, Mia.

listeningParts.title: A new city bike-sharing scheme
listeningParts.contextDescription: A local radio presenter interviews a transport officer about a bike-sharing scheme.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: And now on Morning City, we're talking about the new bike-sharing scheme that starts next month. With me is Rachel Lim from the city council's transport department. Rachel, welcome.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.text: Thanks for having me.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: So, for listeners who haven't heard about it, what exactly is the scheme?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.text: Well, from the first of May, people will be able to hire a bicycle from any of our docking stations around the city, ride it wherever they want to go, and leave it at another station. It's designed mainly for short journeys, the kind of trip that's a bit too far to walk but where taking the car is a waste of time and fuel.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: How many bikes are we talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.text: We're starting with six hundred bikes at forty stations. A third of them are electric, which should help people who are worried about the hills on the north side of the city. If the first year goes well, we'd like to double the number of stations.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: Why start with this number? Some people have said it's rather small for a city of our size.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.text: It's deliberately what we call a pilot scheme. We'd rather start with fewer stations in the right places and learn from how people use them than spread the bikes too thinly. Other cities have found that if a station is often empty when people need a bike, they quickly give up on the scheme altogether. The operator will also move bikes around in vans during the day to stop the busiest stations running out.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: And how do people pay?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.text: Everything is done through a phone app. You can pay per ride, which costs one pound to unlock the bike and then ten pence a minute, or you can buy an annual membership for sixty pounds, which gives you unlimited rides of up to forty-five minutes. Electric bikes cost a little more on both options. For people without a smartphone, we'll also have a card, available from the main library.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: Now, a lot of cities have tried schemes like this, and some have had problems. Bikes left everywhere, blocking pavements...

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.text: Yes, that's mostly with what are called dockless schemes, where you can leave the bike anywhere. We deliberately chose a system with fixed stations. You have to return the bike to a dock, otherwise the app keeps charging you. That should keep the streets tidy.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: Where will the stations be?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.text: We looked at where people actually travel. So there are stations at both railway stations, at the hospital, at the university campus, in the main shopping streets and in several residential areas. The busiest, we expect, will be the one outside Central Station.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: What about safety? Some people say our roads just aren't safe for cyclists.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.text: That's a fair point, and it's the thing people raised most often in our public consultation. Alongside the scheme, we're building eight kilometres of new protected cycle lanes, separated from traffic by a kerb. The first section, along the riverside, opens at the same time as the scheme. We also recommend helmets, although they're not compulsory, and every bike has lights that switch on automatically.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: Who's paying for all this?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.text: The bikes and stations are provided by a private operator, which collects the fees. The council's main contribution is the cycle lanes, which are funded by a national government grant, so there's no increase in local taxes.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: And finally, Rachel, what would count as success?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.text: Our target for the first year is a million rides. But really, what we'd like to see is fewer short car journeys in the city centre. We'll be measuring traffic levels before and after, and we'll publish the results.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: Rachel Lim, thank you very much.

listeningParts.title: Analysing a commuting survey
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two geography students, Kofi and Emma, discuss the results of a survey they carried out on commuting.

dialogue.speaker: Emma
dialogue.text: Right, Kofi, I've put all the questionnaire results into the spreadsheet. Shall we go through them before we start writing?

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: Yes, please. How many people did we get in the end?

dialogue.speaker: Emma
dialogue.text: Two hundred and thirty-four. Fewer than we'd hoped, but more than enough for the assignment.

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: Okay. And what did we find on journey times? I remember a lot of people complaining when we were handing out the forms.

dialogue.speaker: Emma
dialogue.text: The average one-way journey was thirty-eight minutes. But that hides a big difference. People who drove took about thirty minutes on average, while bus users took nearly fifty.

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: That's not surprising. The buses go round every housing estate. What about satisfaction? We asked people to rate their commute from one to ten.

dialogue.speaker: Emma
dialogue.text: This is the interesting bit. You'd expect drivers to be happiest, since they're quickest. But actually, the cyclists and walkers were the most satisfied, even though some of them had journeys of forty minutes or more.

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: That fits with what I read in that study from Canada. The researchers said that active commuting makes people feel more relaxed when they arrive at work. Drivers spend their whole journey worrying about traffic.

dialogue.speaker: Emma
dialogue.text: And bus users were the least satisfied of all. In the comments, the main complaint wasn't the journey time but the reliability. People said they never knew when the bus would actually come.

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: Did the train users say anything similar?

dialogue.speaker: Emma
dialogue.text: Not really. There weren't many of them, only about twenty, and they were mostly positive, apart from the price of tickets. A few mentioned that trains were crowded at peak times, but they still said they'd rather take the train than drive into the centre and pay for parking.

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: Twenty is too few to say much, though. We should point that out rather than make claims about train users in general.

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: We should definitely include some of those comments. They make the numbers more real. Now, what about our question on flexible working?

dialogue.speaker: Emma
dialogue.text: Forty-one per cent said their employer let them work from home at least one day a week. And most of those said they'd moved further from their workplace in the last five years.

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: So working from home might actually be making commutes longer on the days people do go in. That's a nice point for our discussion.

dialogue.speaker: Emma
dialogue.text: I thought so too. Though we can't prove that one causes the other from a survey like ours.

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: True. We'll need to be careful how we word it. Okay, so what are the weaknesses we should mention?

dialogue.speaker: Emma
dialogue.text: The biggest one, I think, is where we collected the data. We stood outside the train station and the main shopping centre, so we probably got too many people who use public transport, and very few people who drive straight to an out-of-town business park.

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: Yes. And the timing. We only did it on weekday mornings, so shift workers were missed. Anyone who starts work at six wouldn't have been there.

dialogue.speaker: Emma
dialogue.text: Good point. I hadn't thought of that. Also, some people filled in the form very quickly. A few gave the same answer to every question, so I removed those.

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: How many did you take out?

dialogue.speaker: Emma
dialogue.text: Eleven. They're not included in the two hundred and thirty-four.

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: Okay, we need to explain that in the method section. Right, how shall we divide up the writing?

dialogue.speaker: Emma
dialogue.text: Why don't you do the literature review, since you've read the Canadian study and the others, and I'll do the results section, because I've been working with the spreadsheet.

dialogue.speaker: Kofi
dialogue.text: Fine. And let's both do the conclusion together. Can we meet again on Monday to put it all together?

dialogue.speaker: Emma
dialogue.text: Monday's good. In the library, at two?

listeningParts.title: The history of public parks
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in an urban history course.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Today I'd like to talk about the public park, something most of us take completely for granted. But the idea that a city should provide open green space, free for everyone to use, is actually quite recent. For most of history, the large gardens in and around cities belonged to kings, aristocrats or the church, and ordinary people were either kept out or allowed in only on certain days.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The modern public park really begins in the nineteenth century, and the main driving force was not beauty but health. Industrial cities in Britain were growing at an astonishing rate. Manchester's population, for example, increased about six times in the first half of the century. Housing was crowded, the air was full of smoke, and diseases such as cholera spread rapidly. Doctors and reformers believed, partly correctly, that fresh air and open space would reduce disease. Parks were often described at the time as the lungs of the city.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: There was also a moral argument. Many reformers worried that working people spent their only free day, Sunday, in pubs. A park, they argued, would offer a healthier and more respectable alternative. So from the start, parks came with a lot of rules: no gambling, no drinking, and in some cases no walking on the grass.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: One of the first parks created specifically for the public was Birkenhead Park, near Liverpool, which opened in 1847. It was designed by Joseph Paxton, who later designed the Crystal Palace. What was unusual about Birkenhead was the way it was paid for. The town bought far more land than it needed for the park itself and then sold plots around the edges for expensive houses. The sale of those plots covered the cost of building the park.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Birkenhead had a direct influence across the Atlantic. In 1850, an American farmer and journalist called Frederick Law Olmsted visited it and was very impressed, particularly by the fact that rich and poor used it equally. A few years later, Olmsted and the architect Calvert Vaux won the competition to design Central Park in New York. Central Park was enormous, over three hundred hectares, and although it looks natural, almost everything in it was planned. The lakes were dug by hand, millions of trees were planted, and the roads for carriages were sunk below the level of the paths so that walkers wouldn't see the traffic.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In the twentieth century, the purpose of parks changed. Instead of quiet walking, the emphasis moved to active recreation: sports fields, playgrounds and swimming pools. During the two world wars, many parks in Britain were dug up and turned into allotments where people grew vegetables, because of food shortages.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Then, from the 1970s, many cities faced budget cuts, and parks were often among the first things to suffer. Park keepers were removed, and some parks became neglected and were seen as unsafe. More recently, however, there's been a revival of interest. Research has linked access to green space with lower stress and better mental health, and cities are now looking at parks as a way to cope with climate change, because trees and grass reduce temperatures and absorb rainwater that would otherwise cause flooding.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: One of the most talked-about recent examples is the High Line in New York, which opened in 2009 on an old elevated railway line. Instead of demolishing the structure, the city turned it into a long, narrow park above the streets. It's been hugely popular, but it's also been criticised, because it pushed up property prices in the surrounding area, so that some long-term residents could no longer afford to live there. That tension between parks as a public good and parks as a driver of rising prices is something we'll come back to next week.

readingPassages.title: Going underground
paragraphs: In the middle of the nineteenth century, London was the largest city in the world, and its streets were close to gridlock. Every morning, hundreds of thousands of workers poured into the City, the financial district, on foot, by horse-drawn omnibus or in private carriages. The mainline railway companies, which had built their terminals around the edge of the centre, were not permitted to bring their lines further in, so passengers arriving by train simply added to the crowds trying to cross the city by road. One survey in the 1850s counted more than seven hundred thousand people entering the City each day, and journeys of a few kilometres could take well over an hour.

The idea of solving this problem by putting a railway beneath the streets was promoted above all by Charles Pearson, a lawyer who worked for the City of London. Pearson argued for years that an underground line linking the mainline stations would relieve congestion and allow working people to live in healthier suburbs and travel to their jobs. Many people regarded the plan as absurd. Critics warned that tunnels would collapse, that passengers would be poisoned by smoke, and that the noise of trains would disturb the dead in the cemeteries the line would pass close to.

Construction of the Metropolitan Railway began in 1860. Rather than boring deep tunnels, the engineers used a method known as cut and cover. A deep trench was dug along the line of an existing road, the track was laid at the bottom, and the trench was then roofed over with a brick arch and the road rebuilt on top. The method was relatively cheap and avoided the need to buy expensive buildings, but it caused enormous disruption to traffic and businesses while the work was going on, and it meant that the line could only follow the routes of streets wide enough to be dug up.

The line opened on 10 January 1863, running about six kilometres between Paddington and Farringdon. It was an immediate success: almost forty thousand passengers used it on the first day, and in its first year it carried nine and a half million people. The trains were pulled by steam locomotives, and although they were designed to reduce smoke in the tunnels, the stations were notoriously dirty and the air unpleasant. Some passengers nevertheless claimed that the sulphurous atmosphere was good for their health. Charles Pearson did not live to see the result; he had died a few months before the opening.

Over the following decades, further lines were built, but cut and cover had clear limits. The next great advance came with the tunnelling shield, a large iron cylinder that protected workers as they dug through the London clay, allowing tunnels to be bored deep below the surface without disturbing the streets above. These deep tubes, which gave the system its popular nickname, could not have used steam engines, because there was no way to remove the smoke. The first deep line, the City and South London Railway, opened in 1890 and used electric trains from the start.

Electricity transformed the system. By the early years of the twentieth century, the older lines had also been converted to electric power, and a series of new tube lines was built, many of them financed by the American businessman Charles Yerkes. Investors, however, often lost money, because fares were kept low and the lines were expensive to build. In 1933, the various private companies were brought together into a single public body, the London Passenger Transport Board, which was responsible for the Underground as well as buses and trams.

The London Underground served as a model for cities around the world. Budapest opened a line in 1896, followed by Paris in 1900, Berlin in 1902 and New York in 1904. Today more than one hundred and eighty cities have metro systems, and the largest of them, in cities such as Shanghai and Beijing, now carry far more passengers than London. Yet many of the basic features of underground railways, from the shape of tunnels to the use of a simplified diagrammatic map, can still be traced back to the system that began beneath the streets of Victorian London.

readingPassages.title: Forests in the sky
paragraphs: When the two residential towers known as the Bosco Verticale, or Vertical Forest, were completed in Milan in 2014, they attracted attention from around the world. The buildings, designed by the architect Stefano Boeri, are covered with around nine hundred trees and more than twenty thousand smaller plants, growing on large balconies that project from every floor. Boeri has said that the total planting is equivalent to about two hectares of forest, squeezed onto a footprint of less than a quarter of a hectare. Since then, similar projects have been built or planned in cities from Sydney to Singapore, and the image of a tower draped in greenery has become a familiar symbol of the sustainable city, appearing in architectural competitions and property advertisements alike.

Supporters of such buildings point to a range of benefits. Plants absorb carbon dioxide and some air pollutants, and they release moisture through their leaves, which cools the air around them. On a hot summer day, a planted facade can be several degrees cooler than bare concrete or glass, reducing the need for air conditioning in the apartments behind it. Trees and shrubs also provide shelter from wind and noise, and they create habitats for birds and insects in places where nature is otherwise scarce. Surveys of residents suggest that many people simply enjoy living surrounded by plants, and there is growing evidence that contact with greenery reduces stress.

Building a forest in the sky, however, is far from simple. Trees are heavy, especially when their soil is wet, and balconies must be designed to carry much greater loads than usual, which requires extra concrete and steel. The Milan towers needed specially reinforced structures, and engineers tested the trees in a wind tunnel to make sure that they would not be blown over in storms. Each tree is attached to the building with steel cables, and its roots grow in containers rather than in open ground, which limits how large it can become.

Maintenance is another major issue. The plants must be watered, fed and pruned, and dead trees must be replaced. In Milan, this work is carried out by specialist gardeners who abseil down the outside of the buildings several times a year, and the costs are included in the residents' service charges. An automatic irrigation system delivers water to every container, much of it recycled from the buildings themselves. Critics argue that this level of care makes vertical forests an option only for wealthy residents, and indeed apartments in the Milan towers are among the most expensive in the city.

There are also questions about the environmental balance. The extra concrete and steel needed to support the trees have a substantial carbon footprint, since producing cement is a major source of greenhouse gas emissions. Some researchers have calculated that the trees on a single tower absorb only a small fraction of the carbon released in constructing the reinforced structure, and that it may take many decades, if ever, for the planting to make up the difference. From this perspective, a park at ground level, or trees planted along streets, may deliver far greater benefits for the same cost.

Defenders of the concept respond that the comparison is unfair, because the purpose of vertical forests is not simply to store carbon. In dense cities, they argue, land at ground level is extremely scarce, and a planted tower adds green space where none would otherwise exist. They also point to newer designs that reduce the structural cost, for example by using lighter timber frames, choosing smaller species of tree or concentrating planting on lower floors. Boeri himself has developed versions of the idea for social housing in the Netherlands, with the aim of showing that vertical greenery need not be a luxury.

What seems clear is that vertical forests are not a solution on their own. Their greatest contribution may be symbolic: by making greenery highly visible in the skyline, they have encouraged city authorities, developers and the public to think more seriously about integrating nature into urban design. Whether the next generation of buildings will be covered in trees, or simply surrounded by better streets and parks, will depend on careful assessment of costs and benefits rather than on striking images alone.

readingPassages.title: The wisdom and madness of crowds
paragraphs: For much of the twentieth century, the dominant view of crowds was deeply pessimistic. Its most influential source was a book published in 1895 by the French writer Gustave Le Bon, who argued that individuals who join a crowd lose their capacity for reason. Submerged in the mass, he claimed, a person descends several rungs on the ladder of civilisation, becoming impulsive, suggestible and potentially violent. Le Bon's ideas were enormously popular, and they shaped how police forces, politicians and the public thought about crowds for decades. Even today, news reports routinely describe crowds as 'stampeding' or 'panicking' in emergencies, as though people in large groups behave like frightened animals.

Over the past forty years, however, researchers have assembled a very different picture. A key figure in this work is the British psychologist John Drury, who has studied how people actually behaved in emergencies ranging from fires and shipwrecks to terrorist attacks. His conclusion, based on interviews with survivors and analysis of video footage, is that mass panic is extremely rare. In most disasters, people do not trample one another in a selfish rush to escape. Instead, they tend to help strangers, wait their turn and cooperate, often at considerable risk to themselves. Where deaths do occur in crowds, they are usually caused by the physical pressure of too many bodies in a confined space, not by irrational behaviour.

To explain this, Drury and his colleagues draw on what is known as social identity theory. According to this approach, a crowd is not simply a collection of individuals who happen to be in the same place. When people face a shared threat, they often begin to see themselves as part of a common group, a 'we' rather than a collection of separate 'I's. This shared identity encourages people to trust one another and to care about what happens to others in the group. In other words, far from losing their identity in a crowd, people often gain a new one, and it is this that guides their behaviour.

These ideas have important practical consequences. If authorities assume that crowds are likely to panic, they may withhold information in an emergency, fearing that the truth will cause chaos. Research suggests the opposite approach is more effective: people respond better when they are given clear, honest information about what is happening and what they should do. Similarly, if police treat an entire crowd as a threat because of the actions of a small minority, they risk creating the very conflict they wish to avoid. Studies of football crowds and protests have found that heavy-handed policing can cause previously peaceful participants to unite against the police, whereas approaches that distinguish between troublemakers and the majority tend to reduce violence.

A separate line of research has focused on a more surprising idea: that crowds can sometimes be wiser than individuals. The classic illustration dates from 1906, when the scientist Francis Galton attended a country fair where visitors were invited to guess the weight of an ox. Galton, who had expected ordinary people to perform poorly, collected around eight hundred guesses and found that their average was within one per cent of the true weight, closer than almost any individual guess. Later research has repeated this effect for many kinds of estimate, from the number of sweets in a jar to the outcome of elections.

The wisdom of crowds, however, depends on certain conditions. The most important is independence: each person must make their own judgement without being influenced by others. When people can see each other's answers, or are exposed to the same misleading information, their errors stop cancelling out and instead reinforce one another. In one experiment, participants who were shown the estimates of others became more confident while their collective accuracy actually fell. This helps to explain why groups that discuss a problem at length can sometimes reach worse decisions than the same people would have reached alone, a phenomenon sometimes called groupthink.

I would suggest that the two bodies of research share an important lesson. Neither the old idea of the mindless mob nor a naive faith in collective wisdom captures how groups really work. Crowds can be cooperative or hostile, accurate or deeply mistaken, depending on how their members see themselves and how they are treated. Understanding those conditions is not merely of academic interest; it is essential for anyone who has to manage large gatherings or make decisions on behalf of others.
